newsitem.title: USA: Kansas wheat tour to observe freeze damaged sites.
newsitem.headline: Kansas wheat tour to observe freeze damaged sites.

text.p: About 60 people next week are slated to visit a variety of wheat fields in Kansas including the areas damaged by a freeze the weekend of April 12-13.

"I don't know how severe the freeze was. You can hear everything," said Ben Handcock, Executive Vice President of the Wheat Quality Council, the producer and processor organization responsible for the annual crop evaluation tour.
But Handcock did say he didn't think the freeze was "as bad as some thought because a lot of wheat was planted late in southwest Kansas."
The later seeded crop did not suffer as great a loss as the early planted fields because the crop was not as mature and therefore not as vulnerable to winterkill.

The southwest corner of Kansas plus the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles were the areas most severely affected by the weekend cold snap. A wide range of estimates of the freeze loss, from 50 million bushels to 300 million bushels including all states, circulated following the memorable weekend.
A separate tour group including Jerry Gidel, Chicago-based grain analyst for Dean Witter, will tour the hard-hit wheat growing regions of Texas and Oklahoma.

Before the freeze, Gidel was estimating a total U.S. hard red winter wheat crop of 980 million bushels but his estimate now is at 850 million bushels. "Originally I took off 170 million bushels (because of the freeze) but am now at 130 million bushels lost," Gidel said.

Doane Agriculture Services wheat marketing director Bill Nelson early in the year pegged the hard red winter wheat crop this year in the U.S. at one billion bushels but has shaved 150 million bushels from that tally. But the St Louis, Missouri-based Nelson did say he would be surprised if the crop damage was less than his projections.

"I respect some of the people who say the damage was up to 200 to 300 million bushels," Nelson said. "There is still a lot of argument as to the extent of damage to the crop. We'll have to wait to May and June to assess the damage.
Last year the Kansas wheat crop totaled 255.2 million bushels, Oklahoma 93.1 million and Texas 75.4 million bushels, according to the U.S. Agriculture Department.
The Kansas wheat tour begins Monday in Manhattan, Kansas and ends Thursday afternoon at the Kansas City Board of Trade where the group will release its production estimate for Kansas.
